The hardware is given only as 'MacBook Pro, Intel Core i7, 3.3 GHz, 2 cores' with no CPU model, so it is not A; the benchmark is first-party (same org), so C.

corrections.claimed_speedup: 1 field ($._id.$oid): pikkr 954.1471 MB/s (basic parsing only) and 1424.6397 MB/s (speculative, train_num=100) vs serde_json 452.4017 MB/s (~2.1x / ~3.1x); 16 fields: pikkr 815.7086 MB/s (basic) and 966.4520 MB/s (speculative) vs serde_json 231.7726 MB/s (~3.5x / ~4.2x). MB/s values verbatim from benchmark README output; ratios derived from page data.
corrections.compiler_and_flags: rustc 1.22.0-nightly (d93036a04 2017-09-07), cargo 0.23.0-nightly (34c0674a2 2017-09-01) per pikkr README; bench.sh builds with RUSTFLAGS="-C target-cpu=native" cargo build --release; serde_json 1.0.3, json 0.11.9, pikkr 0.16.0 (Cargo.lock)
corrections.hardware: MacBook Pro, Intel Core i7 3.3 GHz, 1 processor / 2 cores, 256 KB L2 per core, 4 MB L3, 16 GB RAM (exact CPU model not stated)
corrections.caveats: Abandoned since 2017-09-21 (no commits in ~9 years); requires nightly Rust and an AVX2 CPU, and the 2017 nightly code may not build with current rustc. First-party benchmark on a single dataset (companies.json concatenated 14x, ~1.09 GB, 263,214 records) whose uniform record structure suits pikkr's Mison-style speculative parsing; the peak numbers need training (train_num=100). The serde_json side is a hand-written DeserializeSeed query extractor that skips unneeded values with IgnoredAny, against serde_json 1.0.3 (2017); current serde_json was not tested. No exact CPU model is given.

notes: All MB/s figures match the benchmark README output and the pikkr README chart; the record's 'RUSTFLAGS default' was wrong (bench.sh sets -C target-cpu=native). Downgraded A to C only because the CPU is named as a generic 'Intel Core i7 3.3 GHz' and the benchmark is first-party; metadata (MIT, 641 stars, last commit 2017-09-21, not archived, not a fork) checks out.

Parse' rows on an i7-4980HQ with clang 7.0; the code is public (src/tests/ujson4ctest.cpp, src/cjsonlibs/ujson4c_all.c) and build/premake5.lua sets release flags (optimize Full, NDEBUG, -march=native). corrections.claimed_speedup: Parse to DOM, citm_catalog.json: ujson4c 1.841 ms vs RapidJSON 1.950 ms and RapidJSON_Insitu 1.922 ms (~1.04-1.06x faster); twitter.json: ujson4c 1.114 ms vs RapidJSON 1.227 ms (~1.10x faster) but slower than RapidJSON_Insitu 0.995 ms; canada.json: ujson4c 5.990 ms vs RapidJSON 4.755 ms (slower). Times verbatim from the CSV; ratios derived from page data.
corrections.workload: nativejson-benchmark '1. Parse' test (parse JSON text into a DOM) on canada.json, citm_catalog.json and twitter.json; ujson4c wins on citm_catalog.json and on twitter.json vs plain RapidJSON.
corrections.compiler_and_flags: clang 7.0, mac64 (per results file name); premake5 gmake 'release' configuration: optimize "Full", NDEBUG, -march=native -Wall -Wextra (build/premake5.lua)
corrections.caveats: 2016 benchmark numbers on old hardware and compiler (clang 7.0); the margin over RapidJSON is small (~4-10%) and workload-specific: it beats plain RapidJSON on citm_catalog.json and twitter.json, beats RapidJSON_Insitu only on citm_catalog.json, and loses on canada.json. It uses about 4x RapidJSON's memory on citm_catalog.json (4,698,144 vs 1,123,008 bytes). nativejson conformance is weak (Parse Double 34/66, Parse String 5/9 correct) and it has no stringify support. The repo is archived; the last commit is 2014-04-08. GitHub reports license NOASSERTION, but LICENSE.txt is BSD-3-Clause text (Electronic Arts), and the bundled decoder carries TCL-derived numeric code.

notes: The citm_catalog numbers match the CSV exactly. The record's claim that ujson4c loses on the other two files was wrong: it also beats plain RapidJSON on twitter.json. last_commit is corrected from 2015-04-21 (that is the repo pushed_at date) to 2014-04-08, the date of the last commit on master.
